what_its_for: Binimetinib is a cancer medicine used to treat a type of skin cancer called melanoma that has spread or cannot be removed by surgery. It is used together with another medicine called encorafenib (Braftovi). It works by blocking certain proteins (MEK1 and MEK2) that help cancer cells grow and divide.
how_to_take: Swallow the tablets whole with a full glass of water. You can take binimetinib with or without food. Take it at the same times each day (morning and evening, about 12 hours apart) to keep a steady level of medicine in your body. Do not crush, chew, or split the tablets.
dosing: The usual adult dose is 45 mg (two 15 mg tablets) taken twice a day, approximately every 12 hours. Always take it exactly as your doctor prescribed. Do not change your dose or stop taking it without talking to your doctor first, even if you feel well.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — BUT only if your next scheduled dose is more than 6 hours away. If it is less than 6 hours until your next dose, skip the missed dose and take the next dose at the regular time. Never take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store binimetinib tablets at room temperature between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep the tablets in their original container with the lid tightly closed. Keep away from moisture and heat. Keep out of reach of children and pets. Do not use tablets past the expiration date printed on the bottle.
what_to_avoid: Avoid becoming pregnant while taking this medicine, as it can harm an unborn baby. Use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 30 days after your last dose. Do not breastfeed during treatment and for at least 3 days after your last dose. Avoid prolonged sun exposure and use sunscreen, as this medicine may make your skin more sensitive to sunlight. Tell your doctor about all other medicines, vitamins, and supplements you take, as some drugs can interact with binimetinib.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: sudden vision changes or vision loss, eye pain or redness, chest pain, shortness of breath, swelling of your legs or ankles, unusual bleeding or bruising, muscle pain or weakness, signs of infection (fever, chills), severe skin rash or skin peeling, yellowing of your skin or eyes, dark urine, or severe nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea. These could be signs of serious side effects that need immediate medical attention.
when_it_works: You may not feel any different right away, as cancer medicines work inside your body over time. Your doctor will schedule regular check-ups, blood tests, eye exams, and heart tests to see how the medicine is working and to check for side effects. Do not stop taking the medicine just because you feel fine — keep taking it as directed until your doctor tells you to stop.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: This medicine can cause serious harm to an unborn baby. Women who can become pregnant must use effective birth control. Do not breastfeed while taking this medicine. Older adults (65 and over): This medicine can be used in older adults, but your doctor will monitor you closely for side effects. Liver or kidney problems: Tell your doctor if you have liver or kidney disease, as your dose may need to be adjusted or your doctor may need to monitor you more closely. Children: The safety and use of this medicine in children has not been established.
